title: Шеф уезжает, а туристы приезжают  (The Chef Leaves and the Tourists Arrive)

segments.t: Having secretly replaced the spoiled snails with contraband ones, Max assures Chef Barinov that the stock in the fridge is in great shape. Expecting no more than a customer or two on a quiet Monday, the Chef leaves for the afternoon—just as a crowd of Chinese tourists arrives.
В холодильнике отличные улитки, я проверял.
Я не понял, что за ерунда?
Извините, пожалуйста, как у вас получится?
Let's walk back through the scene line by line.
'And I had to go buy a brand-new batch.' Max brings out the contrast between 'both' and 'for me' in a few short words.
'You have been given a lot more authority now.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'power' and finishing on 'more'. Timur answers right away.
В холодильнике отличные улитки, я проверял.
'There are excellent snails in the fridge, I checked them myself.' In Russian, the idea of 'fridge' flows naturally into 'to check' without extra filler words.
'Before we manage to sell it all.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'what' before landing on 'we'll sell'.
'Chef, where are you heading off to?' The grammar packs 'chef' and 'where to' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Timur answers right away.
'There will be at most one and a half people here today.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'will' and finishing on 'a person'.
'I will be back in the evening.' Max brings out the contrast between 'in the evening' and 'will' in a few short words.
'Wait, where is everybody?' Chef Viktor raises the pitch on 'all' to turn the phrase into a direct spoken question. Timur answers right away.
'Two huge barges.' Notice how Russian expresses 'two' and 'barge' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
'Oh, come on now.' Max anchors the line on 'yes', while 'really?!' completes the thought.
Я не понял, что за ерунда?
'I do not get it, what kind of nonsense is this?' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'I', while 'trifle' completes the thought. Timur answers right away.
'Oh, take it easy.' In Russian, the idea of 'yes' flows naturally into 'you' without extra filler words.
Извините, пожалуйста, как у вас получится?

'Excuse me, please, how will you manage to seat us?' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'. Let's hear the full exchange one more time at natural speed.

Я не понял, что за ерунда?
Извините, пожалуйста, как у вас получится?

That wraps up this scene as max replaces the spoiled snails just before Chef Barinov leaves for the afternoon expecting a dead Monday, right as busloads of Chinese tourists arrive at Claude Monet. See you next time!
